strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly articulates the latency-accuracy tradeoff in IDE code completion, a genuine practical concern
Novel benchmark contribution: identifies and demonstrates 'future context leakage' in REPOCOD and similar benchmarks with concrete examples; valuable for the research community
Comprehensive experimental methodology: three agent variants with systematic ablations; analysis of both retrieval and prediction components; tests on multiple model sizes and backbones
Thorough comparative analysis: Section G provides valuable LLM-judge-based investigation of why BM25 and RepoMap fail, with concrete failure mode examples and insights
Strong reproducibility: extensive implementation details, prompts, hyperparameter settings, and examples in appendices enable reproduction
Practical efficiency: maintains inference latency (~4.5s) while improving accuracy over baselines, directly addressing IDE latency constraints
weaknesses: Critical synthetic benchmark dependence: all main results use a synthetic leakage-free benchmark created via function removal agent; while addressing leakage, this may introduce artifacts and lack fidelity to real repository evolution; acknowledged 'real-world performance may differ' undermines confidence in reported gains

Deployment practicality underexplored: indexing costs are substantial (~50s per file with Claude 3.5 Sonnet); scaling to large repos problematic; re-indexing strategy is vague ('when changes are large enough') with no concrete criteria or thresholds; cost-benefit analysis absent

Substantial oracle gap suggests fundamental limits: SpecAgent achieves 27.86% vs oracle's 40.20% on Qwen3-8B (42% relative gap); indicates speculative context inherently limited; limited analysis of when/why predictions help or fail

Evaluation scope too narrow: only function completion (not bug fixing, refactoring); 980 test cases from 11 projects; predominantly Python; no multilingual or cross-language evaluation; single-turn completions only
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; unclear if single or multiple runs; variance unreported despite 980 test cases

Comparison fairness concerns: oracle uses inference-time state (with target function); SpecAgent uses synthetic indexing-time state; Table 3 shows inference-time SpecAgent achieves higher rates, suggesting improvements partly reflect benchmark setup rather than method
Limited baseline comparisons: doesn't directly compare to cited recent methods (RepoFuse, R2C2-Coder); missing other retrieval-augmented approaches beyond BM25, RepoMap, dense retrieval

Speculative prediction analysis incomplete: Forecaster Agent often produces incorrect predictions (Figures F.4, F.5); limited investigation into prediction quality, diversity, or when they help vs hurt; optimal composition (3 prediction blocks) not well explained

strengths: Identifies and formally addresses 'future context leakage' in code completion benchmarks—an overlooked but important problem that affects benchmark validity

Well-motivated indexing-time vs. inference-time distinction that is architecturally sound and practical for IDE integration; eliminates inference-time retrieval latency while maintaining fast responses
Strong empirical results: 9-11% absolute gains (48-58% relative) over strong baselines while actually reducing inference latency demonstrates clear practical value
Comprehensive experimental analysis including detailed ablations, LLM-judged cross-method comparisons revealing five key insights for BM25 and seven for RepoMap—actionable findings for the community
Rigorous benchmark construction with iterative validation through function removal agents and scoring agents (Sections 5.2, C.1-C.2)
Extensive reproducibility support: complete implementation details, full prompts, concrete examples in Section F, hyperparameter documentation, and thorough appendix
Clear problem articulation with well-illustrated examples (Figure 2) showing how information leakage persists despite simple AST-based cleaning
weaknesses: Primary evaluation on synthetic agent-cleaned benchmarks rather than real repository states raises serious concerns about real-world applicability; while synthetic cleaning removes leakage, it may introduce unintended artifacts and performance gaps vs. natural repository evolution

Indexing cost (46-49 seconds per file) could be prohibitive for large repositories (10K files = 5-8 hours); re-indexing strategy is underdeveloped and relegated to future work despite being critical for deployment

Unfair baseline comparison: baselines evaluated on original leaky REPOCOD while SpecAgent uses cleaned benchmark; should run baselines on both benchmarks to separately quantify leakage impact vs. method contribution
Large gap to oracle upper bound (27.86% vs. 40.20% for 8B model) suggests significant room for improvement but lacks analysis of what oracle contexts provide that SpecAgent misses
Narrow evaluation scope: single-function completion only; Python-only (REPOCOD); 980 test examples; no evaluation on refactoring, bug fixing, or multi-function scenarios

Heavy dependence on Claude 3.7 Sonnet (closed-source, commercial); Appendix A shows ~5% performance drop with Qwen3-Coder, indicating capability-sensitive results; practical deployment concerns regarding cost, API latency, and data privacy

Limited analysis of forecasting failures: examples show incorrect predictions but no systematic study of when forecasting helps vs. hurts; composition ratio (9 retrieval + 3 prediction) empirically tuned without principled justification
Incomplete error analysis: 72% failure rate on pass@1 not deeply investigated; unclear which code patterns or repository types cause failures or when SpecAgent underperforms leaky baselines
Modest improvements for larger models (9-10% for 30B vs. 10-11% for 8B) with no discussion of diminishing returns pattern, potentially important for practitioners
